newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa may be home for Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa may be home for Christmas.

text.p: Mother Teresa, whose health was said to be improving after heart surgery, could return home for Christmas, hospital officials said on Monday.
"Mother Teresa's vital signs are stable," a team of doctors treating the revered missionary at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre said in a regular medical bulletin.
"The Missionaries of Charity are all eager that Mother Teresa should go home in time for Christmas," A.K. Chatterjee, a clinic administrator, told Reuters. "We have told them we will try to do that."
Missionaries of Charity is the order founded by the Roman Catholic nun, and has 456 homes in 111 nations.
An earlier bulletin said that Mother Teresa, who had been in critical condition after heart surgery on November 29, was alert and cooperative, and that her sense of humour was in evidence.

"Doctors, I think now I am more difficult than critical -- I better go home. I will take Dr Patricia with me," it quoted the 1979 Nobel peace prize winner as saying in a reference to Patricia Aubanel, an American doctor on the medical team.
Mother Teresa, 86, walked a short distance of about 40 feet near the clinic's intensive care unit, supported by two nurses. Later she sat up in a chair and prayed for about half-an-hour.
Doctors said Mother Teresa's health was improving following heart surgery, and some brief pain she experienced overnight was not related to her cardiac trouble.
"Mother Teresa's cardiac status continues to stabilise under close monitoring," a medical bulletin said.
"She's better today. She's blessing everyone," said a member of Missionaries of Charity religious order who visited the nun briefly. "She blessed me. She's very happy."
An earlier bulletin said Mother Teresa had experienced brief discomfort overnight but then went back to sleep.
"There was one (pain), but it had nothing to do with her cardiac status," Chatterjee told reporters, saying it could have been gastric pain.
Earlier, Dr Tarun Praharaj, a member of the medical team, said the pain could have been due to her bronchial pneumonia.
Doctors on Sunday said Mother Teresa had suffered a slight setback and her pneumonia was not responding to treatment.
During the previous week, long-standing lung and kidney problems combined with an irregular heartbeat to complicate her recovery from her third heart surgery in five years.
Over the weekend, doctors decided to postpone a procedure aimed at stabilising Mother Teresa's heartbeat, and wait until she gained strength.
The doctors have warned that Mother Teresa's recovery might take a long time, and that she may never be as active as before.
